entry.title: नमक और मौन
entry.content:
दांडी के रास्ते पर, मार्च 1930। फ़ोटोग्राफ़र अज्ञात; पब्लिक डोमेन, विकिमीडिया कॉमन्स के सौजन्य से।
Read in English

रोशनी से पहले नदी की ठंडक आ जाती है।

साबरमती के किनारे भोर का धुंधलका है। हज़ारों लोग पानी के किनारे कंधे से कंधा मिलाए खड़े हैं, और कोई शोर नहीं है। सूखी सरकंडों में हवा चल रही है, और पकी मिट्टी पर एक बाँस की लाठी की धीमी आवाज़ आ रही है।

लाठी थामे हुए व्यक्ति साठ साल के हैं, बदन पर बस एक मोटे खद्दर का टुकड़ा। वे मुड़कर यह भी नहीं देखते कि पीछे कोई है या नहीं। वे दक्षिण की ओर चल पड़ते हैं, और आप उनके पीछे धूल में पहला कदम रखते हैं।

आप उन अठहत्तर में से एक हैं।

दस दिन पहले उन्होंने वायसराय को लिखा था कि यह होने वाला है। धमकी नहीं, एक चिट्ठी, जो उस तकलीफ़ के लिए माफ़ी मांगते हुए शुरू होती है और उस क़ानून का नाम लेती है जिसे वे तोड़ने वाले हैं। किसी ने सीधा जवाब नहीं दिया। घुटनों के बल मैंने रोटी माँगी थी, और मुझे पत्थर मिला।

इस रास्ते पर कोई किसी से कुछ नहीं छुपा रहा। पूरा सफ़र लगेगा यह समझने में कि यह भोलापन नहीं है। यही योजना है।

बीज का कण

लंदन और दिल्ली किसी दंगे के लिए तैयार बैठे थे, क्योंकि सत्ता को बस यही एक शक्ल समझ आती है। गांधी जी ने अठहत्तर चुने।

धूल भरे मैदान में फैली उस कतार को देखिए। कच्छ का अठारह साल का बुनकर। एक संस्कृत का विद्वान। केरल और बंगाल के किसान, और नेपाल से पूरा रास्ता तय करके आया एक आदमी। आप सबने वादा किया है कि जब लोहे की नोक वाली लाठी आपके कंधे पर पड़ेगी, आप हाथ तक नहीं उठाएंगे।

मैं द्रव गतिकी पर काम करता हूँ, इसलिए यही तस्वीर मेरे ज़हन में आती है। पानी को धीरे-धीरे ठंडा करें, बहुत साफ़ रखें, तो वह जमाव-बिंदु से बहुत नीचे भी तरल बना रहता है, बिल्कुल सामान्य दिखते हुए। फिर उसमें बर्फ़ का एक कण डाल दीजिए। पूरा बर्तन आपकी नज़र से भी तेज़ी से ठोस हो जाता है।

उस कण को श्रेय देने का मन करता है, पर उसने लगभग कुछ नहीं किया। वही कण कमरे के तापमान वाले पानी में डालिए, वह बस पिघल जाता है। जो कुछ हुआ, वह पहले से ही पानी के भीतर था, बस किसी शुरुआत का इंतज़ार था।

आप दस साल से इसी तरह ठंडे किए जा रहे थे। असहयोग आंदोलन, और फिर उसे वापस लेने की शर्म। बारडोली, जहाँ इनकार टिका रहा और सरकार ने पहले आँख झुकाई। दिसंबर में लाहौर, जहाँ शब्द पूर्ण स्वराज बन गया, बिना किसी रास्ते के।

देश शांत नहीं है। देश बस स्थिर है।

अठहत्तर आदमी कभी किसी को आज़ाद नहीं करने वाले थे। वे बस इतने काफ़ी हैं कि कहीं से शुरुआत हो सके।

धूल और चरखा

दूसरे हफ़्ते तक आपके तलवों में छाले पड़ चुके हैं, और वे फटकर गुजरात की बारीक धूल से भर जाते हैं।

दोपहर होते-होते धूप पीतल की चादर की तरह तप उठती है। कोई तालियाँ नहीं बजाता, पर हर गाँव की सीमा पर औरतें कुएँ का पानी लिए खड़ी रहती हैं, और वे कुछ नहीं कहतीं, बस आगे की सड़क पर पानी छिड़क देती हैं ताकि ज़मीन आपके पैर न जलाए।

कतार के आगे, कोई गाता है।

वैष्णव जन तो तेने कहिये जे पीड़ पराई जाणे रे

उसे भगवान का आदमी कहिए जो दूसरे का दर्द अपना समझे।

आगे चल रहे बूढ़े व्यक्ति की चाल कभी धीमी नहीं पड़ती, आधी उम्र के जवानों को भी थका देती है। शाम को गाँव के स्कूल में रुककर, सोने से पहले, उन्हें सूत कातना है, और वे कातेंगे, जबकि दिल्ली में लोग इस बात पर चुटकियाँ ले रहे हैं कि पैदल चलकर कोई राज कैसे बदल सकता है।

तीन सौ छियासी किलोमीटर, चौबीस दिन, साठ की उम्र में। अहमदाबाद से एक घंटे में खारा पानी मिल जाता, चार लाइनों में सिमटी ख़बर बनकर। धीमापन ही असली हथियार है। अब देश का हर अख़बार बाध्य है कि हर दिन एक बूढ़े आदमी के पैदल चलने पर कुछ न कुछ छापे, और सरकार कुछ नहीं कर सकती, क्योंकि चलना कोई अपराध नहीं है।

कुछ और भी हो रहा है जबकि आप चल रहे हैं, बिना किसी आवाज़ के। वे सारे छोटे तनख़्वाहदार लोग जिनके ज़रिए एक साम्राज्य ज़मीन को छूता है, कतार के गुज़रते ही इस्तीफ़ा दे रहे हैं, सूरत ज़िले में अकेले दो सौ सत्ताईस।

बुनियादी खनिज

नमक ही क्यों? उनके अपने साथी भी यह पहली नज़र में समझ नहीं पाए। आसान लड़ाइयाँ तो सामने ही खड़ी थीं।

नमक उस पसीने का स्वाद है जो हल के पीछे आठ घंटे बाद निकलता है, वही चुटकी भर धूसर कण जो दाल की हाँडी में डाला जाता है उस परिवार के हाथों जिसके पास डालने को और कुछ नहीं। राजकुमार और भिखारी, दोनों की ज़ुबान पर वही एक खनिज है।

एक पुराने क़ानून के तहत यह ताज की संपत्ति है, व्यापार की नहीं, चीज़ की ही। समंदर किनारे जाकर धूप में सूखा नमक उठाना भी अपराध है। यह कर सरकार की आमदनी का लगभग बारहवाँ हिस्सा है, और इसे वे लोग चुकाते हैं जो और कोई कर नहीं चुकाते।

यही वह बात है जिसे मैं बार-बार सोचता हूँ। आयकर की सरकार एक वाक्य में ज़ोर से बचाव कर सकती है, और तब भी सरकार जैसी लगती रहती है। अब नमक के क़ानून को ज़ोर से बोलकर देखिए। इसे ईमानदारी से कहने का हर तरीक़ा या तो हास्यास्पद लगता है या क्रूर, कोई तीसरा रास्ता नहीं। वे उस क़ानून की तलाश में नहीं थे जो सबसे ज़्यादा चोट पहुँचाए। वे उस क़ानून की तलाश में थे जो बयान होते ही टिक न पाए।

कीचड़ में हाथ

चौबीस रातें स्कूल के पुआल पर, फिर हवा बदल जाती है, नम और खारी, समंदर की काई की गंध लिए।

पाँच अप्रैल की शाम को आप दांडी पहुँचते हैं। उस रात लगभग कोई नहीं सोता, क्योंकि सुबह होते ही आप उस लकीर को पार करेंगे जहाँ से लौटना नहीं है।

भोर धूसर और शांत है। ज्वार उतर चुका है, पीछे चमकती कीचड़ छोड़ गया है। वे समंदर में उतरकर स्नान करते हैं, फिर उस गड्ढे तक चलते हैं जहाँ धूप ने कच्चे नमक की एक परत सुखा दी है। वे घुटनों के बल बैठते हैं, उंगलियाँ गीली गाद में धँसाते हैं, और मुट्ठी भर मैली, चमकती कीचड़ उठाते हैं।

इसके साथ, मैं ब्रिटिश साम्राज्य की बुनियादों को हिला रहा हूँ।

तेईस ग्राम गीला धूसर नमक। इसे बाद में पाँच सौ पच्चीस रुपये में नीलाम किया जाएगा, लगभग एक क्लर्क की साल भर की तनख़्वाह। यह तब तक कुछ नहीं था, जब तक इसे रखना अपराध नहीं बन गया।

खुलता हुआ स्प्रिंग

आगे जो होता है वह कोई धमाका नहीं है। वह उस चीज़ से कहीं ज़्यादा डरावना है जिससे कोई साम्राज्य डरता है, यानी हालत का बदल जाना। क़ानून टूटता नहीं, वह भाप बनकर उड़ जाता है।

बंबई की बालकनियों पर औरतें समंदर का पानी उबालती हैं। मद्रास के किनारों पर मछुआरे सूखा नमक खुरचकर अजनबियों के हाथों में रख देते हैं। महीने के अंत तक साठ हज़ार लोग जेल में हैं।

पेशावर में एक नेता की गिरफ़्तारी के बाद निहत्थे लोग बाज़ार भर देते हैं। बख़्तरबंद गाड़ियाँ, फिर मशीनगनें, छह घंटे तक। दो टुकड़ियाँ उन बसों में बैठने से मना कर देती हैं जो उन्हें वहाँ ले जानी थीं, और कोर्ट-मार्शल की जाती हैं। अगर आप जानना चाहते हैं कि 1930 में असल में क्या हुआ था, वह सैनिकों का उस बस के पास खड़े रहना है जिसमें वे नहीं चढ़ते।

अगले महीने एक नमक कारख़ाने पर मार्चर कतारों में चढ़ाई करते हैं, यह जानते हुए कि उन्हें पीटा जाएगा और हाथ नहीं उठाना है। वहाँ खड़ा एक पत्रकार लिखता है कि वे यूँ गिरते गए जैसे बॉलिंग के पिन, एक हाथ भी नहीं उठा, लाठियों की आवाज़ जहाँ वह खड़ा था वहाँ तक सुनाई देती रही। उसकी रिपोर्ट तेरह सौ पचास अख़बारों में छपती है और अमेरिकी सीनेट के रिकॉर्ड में पढ़कर सुनाई जाती है।

सबसे हल्का सच

अगले मार्च में हुआ समझौता बहुत छोटा है। क़ैदी छूटते हैं, तटीय इलाक़ों के लोगों को अपने घर के लिए नमक बनाने की इजाज़त मिलती है। नमक कर 1946 तक बना रहता है। आज़ादी 1947 में आती है, बँटी हुई, इतनी मौतों के साथ कि उस सुबह का हिसाब छोटा लगने लगता है। यह सब उस एक तट पर तय नहीं हुआ था, और इसे नकारना बेईमानी होगी।

पर जो वहाँ तय हुआ, उसकी शक्ल देखिए।

एक साम्राज्य जो ख़ुद को पलटनों और युद्धपोतों में गिनता था, उसका जवाब एक बूढ़े की खुली हथेली पर सूखती तेईस ग्राम गीली मिट्टी से दिया गया, और उसके पास इसका कोई जवाब नहीं था। उसका हर हथियार बल से लड़ने के लिए बना था, और बल कभी आया ही नहीं। आप किसी फ़ौज पर गोले दाग सकते हैं। आप किसी शहर को भूखा रख सकते हैं। पर आप क्या करेंगे जब तीस करोड़ लोग एक सुबह उठें, ज़मीन से एक चुटकी मिट्टी उठाएँ, और जीने की इजाज़त माँगना बंद कर दें?

उसने नब्बे हज़ार को गिरफ़्तार किया। थाने भर गए, काग़ज़ ख़त्म हो गए, हर गिरफ़्तारी गिरफ़्तार करने वाले को ही बुरा दिखाने लगी। बंदूकें अपनी जगह रखी रहीं, किसी ने कुछ नहीं तोड़ा, और जो चीज़ दो सौ साल से एक उपमहाद्वीप को थामे हुए थी, जो कभी तोप नहीं थी बल्कि यह विश्वास थी कि विरोध सोचा भी नहीं जा सकता, वह एक सूखी टहनी की तरह, सबसे ख़ामोश तरीक़े से टूट गई।

सत्ता यही भूल जाती है, हर सदी में, और फिर भूलेगी: वह एक भारी हथौड़े के लिए तैयार रहती है, कभी एक हल्की चीज़ के लिए नहीं।

डर के पहाड़ को ग़ुस्से के बड़े पहाड़ से नहीं गिराया जाता। आपको बस वह एक छोटा, सच्चा हिस्सा ढूँढना है जो सबका बराबर का है, उसे छूना है, और बाक़ी दुनिया को अपने आप जागने देना है।

गांधी जी ने बस वह जगह चुनी जहाँ उंगली रखनी थी।

बाक़ी सब आप थे।
entry.summary: सबसे भारी ज़ंजीरें सबसे हल्की चीज़ों से क्यों टूटती हैं।

entry.title: Salt and Silence
entry.content:
On the road to Dandi, March 1930. Photographer unknown; public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
हिंदी में पढ़ें

The chill comes off the river before the light does.

It is the edge of dawn on the banks of the Sabarmati. Thousands stand along the water in the grey, shoulder to shoulder, and nobody is shouting. Just wind in the dry reeds, and the knock of a bamboo staff against baked earth.

The man holding it is sixty, wrapped in one length of coarse white cloth. He does not turn to check who is behind him. He starts walking south, and you step into the dust after him.

You are one of the seventy-eight.

Ten days ago he wrote to the Viceroy to say this was going to happen. Not a threat. A letter that apologises for the trouble it is about to cause, and names the law he means to break. Nobody answered him directly. On bended knees I asked for bread, and I have received stone instead.

Nobody on this road is hiding from anybody. It takes the length of the walk to understand that this is not innocence. It is the design.

The seed crystal

London and Delhi were braced for a riot: ten thousand angry men at a government gate, because that is the only shape power knows how to see. He took seventy-eight.

A teenage weaver from Kutch. A Sanskrit scholar. Farmers from three provinces, and one man who walked the length of Nepal to be here. Every one has promised that when the lathi comes down on his collarbone, he will not lift a hand to stop it.

I work on fluids, so this is the picture I reach for. Cool water slowly, keep it very clean, and it will sit far below freezing and stay liquid, looking like nothing at all. Drop in one grain of ice and the whole vessel goes solid faster than the eye can follow. The grain gets the credit, but it did almost nothing; drop it into water at room temperature and the afternoon just goes on. Everything that happened was already inside the water, waiting for somewhere to start.

The country had been supercooled for ten years: non-cooperation and its shameful collapse, a tax refusal at Bardoli that made the government blink first, a declaration weeks earlier that the goal was now complete independence, with no method attached to it yet.

It was not calm. It was only still.

Seventy-eight men were never going to free anything. They were enough to be a place where something could begin.

The dust and the wheel

By the second week the soles of your feet are blistered, and the blisters tear and fill with dust.

The heat comes down like brass by midday. Nobody applauds. But at the edge of every village, women stand with brass pots of well water and say nothing, only tip the water onto the road so the ground will not burn your feet.

Near the front, someone sings into the wind.

Vaishnava jana to tene kahiye je peed parayi jaane re

Call him a man of God who feels another’s pain as his own.

The old man never slows, his stride quietly finishing off men half his age. At dusk, in a village schoolhouse, you hear the creak of a spinning wheel. Before he sleeps he has thread to spin, and he spins it, while officials in Delhi write home about the comedy of a rebellion on foot.

Three hundred and eighty-six kilometres, twenty-four days, on foot, at sixty. Salt water is an hour from Ahmedabad; he could have broken the law before lunch and been in a cell by dark, four lines on an inside page. The slowness is the instrument. Every newspaper is now obliged to file something, every day, about a man walking, and there is nothing the government can do, because walking is not a crime. Conspiracy needs surprise. This needs the opposite.

Something else moves while you walk, without a sound: the officers through whom an empire touches the ground, resigning as the column passes. Two hundred and twenty-seven, in one district alone.

The universal mineral

Why salt? His own colleagues could not follow it, at first. Easier fights were sitting right there.

Salt is the taste of your own sweat after eight hours behind a plough, the pinch of grey crystal in a family’s last pot of lentils. Prince and beggar carry the same mineral on the tongue.

Under an old law the Crown owns it outright, not the trade in it, the thing itself. Walking to the shore to pick up what the sun already dried on the rock is a crime. The tax is close to a twelfth of the government’s revenue, paid by people who pay nothing else at all.

Here is the part I keep turning over. A government can defend an income tax out loud, in one sentence, and still sound like a government. Say the salt law out loud. Every honest way of putting it comes out either ridiculous or cruel, and there is no third way. He was not hunting for the law that hurt the most. He was hunting for the one that could not survive being described.

The hand in the silt

Twenty-four nights on straw, then the air changes, damp and saline, tasting of kelp. You reach Dandi at dusk. That night almost nobody sleeps: at sunrise you cross a line with no way back.

Dawn is grey and quiet, the tide out, leaving wide flats of shining mud. He walks into the sea, bathes, crosses to a pit where the sun has dried a crust of raw salt, and kneels. His fingers sink into the silt. He lifts a handful of it into the light.

With this, I am shaking the foundations of the British Empire.

Twenty-three grams of wet grey salt. It will later be auctioned for five hundred and twenty-five rupees, about a clerk’s pay for a year. It was worth nothing at all until it became illegal to hold.

The spring uncoiled

What follows is not an explosion. It is something an empire fears more: a change of state. The law does not break, it evaporates. Women boil seawater on balconies in Bombay; fishermen hand strangers salt scraped off rocks near Madras. By month’s end sixty thousand people are in prison. At midnight, they come for him.

In Peshawar, after another leader’s arrest, an unarmed crowd fills a bazaar. Armoured cars, then machine guns, for six hours. Two platoons of Indian soldiers refuse to board the buses that would carry them there, and are court-martialled for it. If you want to know what actually happened in 1930, it is soldiers standing beside a bus they will not get on.

At a salt works the following month, marchers walk forward in columns, told they will be beaten and must not raise a hand. A reporter there writes that they went down like ten-pins, not one arm raised, the clubs audible from where he stood. His dispatch runs in thirteen hundred and fifty newspapers and reaches the floor of the United States Senate.

The lightest truth

The treaty that follows is thin: prisoners released, coastal families allowed to make their own salt. The tax stands until 1946. Freedom, in 1947, comes cut in half, with a death toll that makes this morning’s arithmetic look small. None of that was settled on this beach, and it would be too easy to pretend otherwise.

But look at the shape of what was settled.

An empire that counted itself in battalions and battleships was answered by twenty-three grams of wet mud in an old man’s open hand, and it had nothing to answer with. Every instrument it owned was built to meet force, and force never arrived. You can shell an army. You can starve a city. What do you do when three hundred million people rise one morning, take a pinch of dirt off the ground, and stop asking permission to be alive?

It arrested ninety thousand; the stations filled, the paper ran out, and every arrest made the arresting look worse. The guns stayed racked, nobody stormed anything, and the thing that had held a subcontinent still for two hundred years, never the artillery but the belief that resistance was unthinkable, snapped like a dry twig, in near silence.

That is what power forgets, every century, and will forget again: it prepares for a heavier hammer, never a lighter one.

You do not bring down a mountain of fear by piling up a mountain of anger. You find the one small true thing that belongs to everybody equally, and you touch it, and let the rest of the world wake up on its own.

He only chose the place to put his finger.

The rest of it was you.
entry.summary: Why the heaviest chains are broken by the lightest things.

entry.title: Self-Learning in the Age of AI

link.title: Self-Learning in the Age of AI

entry.content:
I did okay in school by memorising. Good enough marks that everyone assumed I understood what I was doing.

I didn’t. The mathematics I “did” was a set of algorithms I could execute — push symbols through algebra, get the right answer out. Ask me why and there was nothing there. I don’t blame my school; plenty of classmates came out of the same rooms thinking perfectly well. The shortcut was there and it worked, so I took it every time.

Then school ended, I looked properly, and there wasn’t much inside.

Oliver Byrne's 1847 edition of Euclid's Elements replaced lettered labels with colour, so a proof could be followed by looking at it. Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.

Starting over, alone

I took a break after school and joined a local college for a Bachelor of Science, five minutes from home. Classes were irregular and I wasn’t showing up either, but it gave me the thing I’d never had: unstructured time. Luck, not merit.

By the second year — 2017 — I decided to start from zero, and asked my parents for a broadband connection. I’d had a phone for years, so what changed wasn’t access. It was that I finally wanted something from it.

I found the Chicago undergraduate mathematics bibliography, which tells you book by book what’s worth reading and why. After that, my pocket money each month became one classic, or printouts of something I couldn’t afford. The rest I pirated. And I went back to the beginning — algebra, geometry, Euclid, then physics, working problems in order for the first time in my life.

The lectures mattered just as much. MIT OpenCourseWare, Open Yale Courses, NPTEL — whole courses, taught properly, sitting there for free. Watching someone good work through a derivation on a blackboard, changing their mind mid-way, was the closest thing to a classroom I’d ever had. I still don’t think people appreciate what those projects did, or how quietly they did it.

What got me most, though, wasn’t the formulas. It was the stories: people struggling with one idea for a century, getting it wrong in interesting ways, until someone finally saw it. It had never occurred to me that mathematics had a plot.

That was the happiest I’ve been about learning.

Where I got stuck

It didn’t last, and the reasons are mostly about me. My gaps were large and I couldn’t tell which ones were missing, so easy problems stopped me dead. Spivak’s chapter on limits took me apart — not “this is difficult,” more like “maybe I’m not built for this.”

There was nobody to ask. Stack Exchange helped more than I can say, but it isn’t a conversation. You can’t say “wait, go back, why is that step allowed” four times in a row, or admit at 2am that you don’t understand what a limit is for.

I never finished those books. Not one, I think. The self-study did get me into a Master of Science at IIT Kanpur, where a year went past too fast for me to account for — my gaps, not the institute’s fault.

The PhD, and a laboratory

The story gets better, so I should say so. Nobody was going to examine me next Tuesday, so I could read one book slowly and finish it. I was never incapable of reading properly; I’d only ever tried while being timed.

The bigger part was computation. I work on turbulence, so most of what I do is simulation, and at some point it stopped being a way to get numbers and became a laboratory. Switch off gravity. Hold everything still and watch one mode grow. Drop a term and see what breaks. For someone who has to see a mechanism before symbols mean anything, that was the instrument I’d been missing my whole life.

It also killed an assumption I’d carried since school: that understanding is one object, the picture the textbook points at, which you either have or don’t. We write it down the same way, and that shared notation is what lets us check each other — but what happens in your head when you read it is yours. Some see pictures, some see algebra moving, some hear a story. The written form is public; the perception is always subjective.

So “I’m not good at this” is usually a mistranslation. The idea hasn’t been put into the dialect that person thinks in, and I spent years reading that mismatch as a verdict on me.

None of which is a new thought — good teachers have known it forever. I’m writing it down because of what changed next.

The asking got cheap

What I needed in 2017 and couldn’t get was someone patient to ask. That’s now available to almost anyone with a connection, at any hour, free or close to it.

I can ask stupid questions. I can say “explain this like someone who thinks in pictures,” then “no, try a physical example,” and go round again. A book can’t do that, and neither can a lecture, however good — both have committed to one way of explaining, and if that way doesn’t fit your head you’re on your own. Though all of it is made out of books and lectures, so I should be careful calling it better than them. What’s new isn’t the knowledge; it’s that the knowledge answers back.

And what matters to me isn’t how capable these things are. It’s the price. Someone in a town with no good college can ask about school algebra or graduate physics at 2am and get a patient answer. In 2017 that cost me a broadband connection and a lot of luck.

But teachers matter more than any of this

It would be easy to write a triumphant paragraph here and be wrong. This worked for me because I already wanted it badly and knew roughly what to look for. A patient answering machine is useless to someone who doesn’t yet know what to want, and the wanting is almost always put there by a person.

I’ve never seen software make anyone care about something. I’ve seen teachers do it constantly. Someone who notices you’ve gone quiet. Someone who says try the harder problem, and means it, and is right. Someone whose standards you take on as your own without noticing. That isn’t information transfer — it’s a relationship, and it works because there’s a person on the other end whose regard you want.

So as information gets cheap, teachers get more important, not less. Supplying answers used to be the job; now what’s scarce is judgment, attention, and someone who knows you. And this isn’t only about physics or mathematics. We aren’t brains being loaded with content, and most of what carries a person through years of difficulty is other people.

So the structure has to change

If explanation is cheap and abundant, organising education around delivering explanations is a strange use of scarce human hours. I don’t have a proposal — I’m suspicious of anyone who does this early — but the questions seem unavoidable. What is a lecture for now? What is an exam measuring, when the answer is a sentence away? If teachers no longer spend most of their hours on delivery, the best use of those hours is probably noticing individual people: the thing they’ve never had time for and nothing else can do.

Research too. A PhD used to be paid for largely in time — finding what’s known, writing the code, grinding the derivation. As that gets cheaper, what’s left is taste: asking a question worth asking, sensing when a result smells wrong. We’ve never really taught that. You absorb it from an advisor, if you’re lucky in who you get.

I should admit a bias here. Pedagogy is a large part of why I wanted to be in research at all — not only the physics, but the question of how a person actually comes to understand something. That has always looked to me like one of the most interesting problems there is, and right now it also looks like an open one.

So I’d argue this gets rethought deliberately, by people who actually teach, rather than drifting into whatever shape it takes by default.

Where I am

I still don’t understand very much — the longer you do this, the more precisely you see the shape of what you don’t know. What I have back is the excitement. I get to be the person from 2017 again, except now when I get stuck I don’t have to stay stuck for three weeks and quietly close the book.

If any of this reaches someone stuck where I was at nineteen: the wall is probably not you. Find someone to ask — a person if you can, and there’s now something patient for 2am when there’s nobody. The second is not a replacement for the first.

Understanding the fundamental laws of the universe, and the abstract things that are beautiful for no practical reason at all, I used to file under “for other people.” I don’t think it belongs there.
entry.summary: A broadband connection in 2017, a pile of books, and years of getting stuck alone. What I think was actually missing.

This is how a post with tabs looks like. Note that the tabs could be used for different purposes, not only for code.

Content 1

{% endtab %}

Content 2

{% endtab %}

{% endtabs %}

With this you can generate visualizations like:

  • js
  • ruby

  • console.log("hello");

Another example

  • json

  - "whatsup"
  - "hi"

entry.title: a post with pseudo code
entry.content:
This is an example post with some pseudo code rendered by pseudocode. The example presented here is the same as the one in the pseudocode.js documentation, with only one simple but important change: everytime you would use $, you should use $$ instead. Also, note that the pseudocode key in the front matter is set to true to enable the rendering of pseudo code. As an example, using this code:

```pseudocode
% This quicksort algorithm is extracted from Chapter 7, Introduction to Algorithms (3rd edition)
\begin{algorithm}
\caption{Quicksort}
\begin{algorithmic}
\PROCEDURE{Quicksort}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \IF{$$p < r$$}
        \STATE $$q = $$ \CALL{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, p, q - 1$$}
        \STATE \CALL{Quicksort}{$$A, q + 1, r$$}
    \ENDIF
\ENDPROCEDURE
\PROCEDURE{Partition}{$$A, p, r$$}
    \STATE $$x = A[r]$$
    \STATE $$i = p - 1$$
    \FOR{$$j = p$$ \TO $$r - 1$$}
        \IF{$$A[j] < x$$}
            \STATE $$i = i + 1$$
            \STATE exchange
            $$A[i]$$ with $$A[j]$$
        \ENDIF
        \STATE exchange $$A[i]$$ with $$A[r]$$
    \ENDFOR
\ENDPROCEDURE
\end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

Generates:

You can display diff code by using the regular markdown syntax:

```diff
diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")
```

Which generates:

diff --git a/sample.js b/sample.js
index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")

But this is difficult to read, specially if you have a large diff. You can use diff2html to display a more readable version of the diff. For this, just use diff2html instead of diff for the code block language:

index 0000001..0ddf2ba
--- a/sample.js
+++ b/sample.js
@@ -1 +1 @@
-console.log("Hello World!")
+console.log("Hello from Diff2Html!")

   - `synchronisedScroll`: scroll both panes in side-by-side mode: `true` or `false`, default is `false`
